messages.subject: Dail-Madsen w Gompertz Dynamics Model Statement in JAGS
messages.subject_clean: Dail-Madsen w Gompertz Dynamics Model Statement in JAGS
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I have used unmarked and pCountOpen with gompertz dynamics with a poisson mixture and allowing for immigration to test for evidence of density dependence (no covariates included). Currently, unless I allow immigration (immigration=True), it returns Hessian errors. I am assuming that the model is not converging well and the MLE is not performing great given the low detection probability from my data. For the immigration model, I get Nans on the omega (carrying capacity) parameter. I could manipulate the K parameter, but am cognizant of the run times if I increase K more than I already have (>24 hours). Therefore, I have dove into the deep end (for me) and tried to get this going in a Bayesian framework with JAGS.

I followed what I could from Hostetler and Chandler 2015, Skold and Knape 2018, and Dennis et al. 2006, 2014. I have also reviewed a version of the AHM2 chapter for these models (thanks Andy) and I have managed to reproduce what I understand to be the trend model from unmarked, but not the Gompertz formulation like I would like to implement with the immigration dynamics (because some counts in some years at plots are 0).

I have copied my model statement and code below for my attempt at the gompertz formulation (including annotations and comments) and I am wondering if anyone might have the time or willingness to help shed some light on what I need to do to get this implemented properly. The current error statement is: "Failed check for discrete-valued parameters in distribution dbin". I suspect there is more incorrect than that. I am new to Bayesian and coding in JAGS, so I suspect my syntax is the major issue (maybe that is naive). Any other relevant reading suggestions would be appreciated.

Thanks in advance for your time and consideration.

Matt

# Bundle data

data_matrix <- abdu_umf_matrix

   str(bdata <- list(C = data_matrix, nsites = nrow(data_matrix),
                  nyears = ncol(data_matrix))) # note length added

# Specify model in BUGS language
sink("gompertz_AHM2.jags")
cat("
model {
# Priors
alpha.lam ~ dnorm(0,0.1) # Abundance parameters
phi ~ dunif(0, 100) # App. survival (omega in paper/unmarked) #should be K??
beta.gamma ~ dnorm(0,0.1) # Recruitment model parameter #should be lamda/growth rate?
gamma0 <- exp(beta.gamma)
alpha.p ~ dnorm(0,0.1) # Detection probability parameters
alpha.0 <- logit(alpha.p)

# Likelihood
for(i in 1:nsites){
   # State process: initial condition
   log(lambda[i]) <- alpha.lam
   N[i,1] ~ dpois(lambda[i])

   # State process: transition model
   for(t in 1:(nyears-1)){
      K[i,t+1] ~ dpois(phi) #Omega = carrying capacity?

      #r[i,t+1] ~ dpois(gamma0) # constant recruitment
      r[i,t+1] ~ dpois(N[i,t] * gamma0) # per-capita recruitment/pop growth rate?

      #N[i,t+1] <- S[i,t+1] + R[i,t+1] #Remove this and sub in gompertz formula
      #Hostetler and Chandler gompertz code...
      N[i,t+1] <- N[i,t] * exp(r[i,t+1] * (1 - log(N[i,t] + 1) / log(K[i,t+1] + 1)))

   }
   # Observation process
   for(t in 1:nyears){
         logit(p[i,t]) <- alpha.p
         C[i,t] ~ dbin(p[i,t], N[i,t])
      }
}

# Derived quantities
#Nbar <- mean(N)
#lambar <- mean(lambda)
}
")
sink()

# Initial values, sometimes very challenging
Rst <- apply(data_matrix, c(1,2), max, na.rm = TRUE)
Rst[Rst == '-Inf'] <- 1
Rst[,1] <- NA
Nst <- array(NA, dim = dim(Rst))
tmp <- apply(data_matrix, 1, max, na.rm = TRUE)
tmp[tmp == '-Inf'] <- 2
Nst[,1] <- tmp

# Initial values
inits <- function(){list(r = Rst, N = Nst+1, alpha.lam = rnorm(1, -1,1))}

# Parameters monitored
params <-c("alpha.lam", "phi", "alpha.gamma", "beta.gamma", "sigma.gamma", "gamma0",
"alpha.p", "N", "K", "r")

# MCMC settings
na <- 1000 ; ni <- 70000 ; nt <- 4 ; nb <- 10000 ; nc <- 4

# try different seeds in hopes of getting one that runs
set.seed(299, kind = "Mersenne-Twister")

out4 <- jags(bdata, inits, params, "gompertz_AHM2.jags", n.adapt = na, n.chains = nc,
             n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, parallel = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Here is a "desperation" technique but for your original analysis approach.

If one is getting hessian errors but parameter estimates are still being obtained, then turn it off (se = FALSE) and use bootstrapping to obtain standard errors.  (This is essentially following the advice in the old Henny Youngman joke: Youngman:  "Doc, it hurts when I do this."  Doc:  "Don't do that.")

However, if as you mention that the individual run times are day-long adventures, then it wouldn't be practical.

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

I haven't had a chance to review AHM2 yet, but I compared your JAGS code to our sample code from the 2015 paper, and I may have found the problem. The line:

r[i,t+1] ~ dpois(N[i,t] * gamma0)

should be something like:
r[i,t+1] <- gamma0
and the line

N[i,t+1] <- N[i,t] * exp(r[i,t+1] * (1 - log(N[i,t] + 1) / log(K[i,t+1] + 1)))

should be something like these lines:
muN[i,t] <- N[i,t] * exp(r[i,t+1] * (1 - log(N[i,t] + 1) / log(K[i,t+1] + 1)))
N[i,t+1] ~ dpois(muN[i,t])
See if those changes help.

Jeff

Jeffrey A. Hostetler, PhD
Branch of Assessment and Decision Support
Division of Migratory Bird Management
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeff, Jim, and John,

Thanks for your suggestions, they have all been helpful. John, thanks for your direction of thinking about the derivation of the parameters. I had not switched from recruitment to growth rate in my model. This got me thinking of my other parameters too, which Jeff further pointed to in his reply. I am not attempting to include covariates on any of the parameters, therefore, I think my initial parameterization was overly complex from my attempt at trying to adapt the ES.cov jags code from the 2015 paper (i.e., I just need to specify prior distributions for r and K). I have adjusted the more straight forward gompertz code provided in the supplementary material and added in the immigration dynamics. Because I am trying to estimate gompertz dynamics, I assume that r should always be positive [r~dunif(0,2) in my code, assuming that my population does not double]? Perhaps this is incorrect. In addition, I think I managed to account for immigration dynamics in my model based on the R script for the Ricker model provided in the supplementary material.

I am able to get the model running now, but there is a lot of uncertainty in my parameter estimates and my detection probability is about 0.5 (SD~0.29; code and output below). In addition, I am not reproducing similar estimates from my pcountOpen models, which I would have expected. Could that be that my priors are off? The parameters seem to be fairly sensitive to what I set the prior distributions at and count and K estimates are  0.5 * max of their respective priors. I have run a few iterations of different prior specifications and this is a consistent result (lambda and K are ~0.5 of their priors maximum).  This does not seem right to me, so I assuming I am again off track again.

Would the following explanation be plausible here? The model is struggling to distinguish process from observation error because of too much variation in the count data and to account for that I should either include some covariates on the process or observation components or we simply need better data (e.g., robust design w repeated visits within a year) to estimate the observation process? Or do I just have the syntax wrong still?

Thanks again for your time. Any insight is greatly appreciated.

Thanks,

Matt

# Specify model in BUGS language
sink("gompertz_AHM2.jags")
cat("
model {
# Priors

lambda ~ dunif(0,30) # Abundance
#alpha ~ dunif(0,50) #for negative binomial formulation
#P <- alpha/(alpha+lambda)
K ~ dunif(0, 50) # Carrying Capacity
r ~ dunif(0,2) #Growth Rate
p ~ dunif(0,1) # Detection probability
iota ~ dunif(0,10) #Immigration

# Likelihood
for(i in 1:nsites){
   # State process: initial condition

   N[i,1] ~ dpois(lambda)
   #N[i,1] ~ dnegbin(P/(alpha+lambda))

   # State process: transition model
   for(t in 1:(nyears-1)){

      muN[i,t] <- N[i,t] * exp(r * (1 - log(N[i,t] + 1) / log(K + 1))) + iota #Gompertz w Immigration
      #muN[i,t] <- N[i,t]*exp(r*(1-N[i,t]/K))+iota #For Ricker w Immigration

      N[i,t+1] ~ dpois(muN[i,t])
   }

   # Observation process
   for(t in 1:nyears){

         y[i,t] ~ dbin(p, N[i,t])
      }
}

# Derived quantities
Nbar <- mean(N)

lambar <- mean(lambda)
}
")
sink()

# Initial values
inits <- function(){list(N=Nst, r = runif(1, 0, 2), lambda=runif(1, 0, 30), K=runif(1,1,50),
                         p=runif(1,0,0.5))}

# Parameters monitored
params <-c("lambda", "K", "r", "p", "iota", "Nbar", "lambar")

# MCMC settings
na <- 1000 ; ni <- 100000 ; nt <- 10 ; nb <- 10000 ; nc <- 3

# try different seeds in hopes of getting one that runs
set.seed(299, kind = "Mersenne-Twister")

gomp.jags <- jags(bdata, inits, params, "gompertz_AHM2.jags", n.adapt = na, n.chains = nc,

             n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, parallel = TRUE)

print(gomp.jags)

> >    # State process: initial condition
> >    log(lambda[i]) <- alpha.lam
> >    N[i,1] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
> >
> >    # State process: transition model
> >    for(t in 1:(nyears-1)){
> >       K[i,t+1] ~ dpois(phi) #Omega = carrying capacity?
> >
> >       #r[i,t+1] ~ dpois(gamma0) # constant recruitment
> >       r[i,t+1] ~ dpois(N[i,t] * gamma0) # per-capita recruitment/pop growth rate?
> >
> >       #N[i,t+1] <- S[i,t+1] + R[i,t+1] #Remove this and sub in gompertz formula
> >       #Hostetler and Chandler gompertz code...
> >       N[i,t+1] <- N[i,t] * exp(r[i,t+1] * (1 - log(N[i,t] + 1) / log(K[i,t+1] + 1)))
> >
> >
> >    }
> >    # Observation process
> >    for(t in 1:nyears){
> >          logit(p[i,t]) <- alpha.p
> >          C[i,t] ~ dbin(p[i,t], N[i,t])
> >       }
> > }
> >
> > # Derived quantities
> > #Nbar <- mean(N)
> > #lambar <- mean(lambda)
> > }
> > ")
> > sink()
> >
> > # Initial values, sometimes very challenging
> > Rst <- apply(data_matrix, c(1,2), max, na.rm = TRUE)
> > Rst[Rst == '-Inf'] <- 1
> > Rst[,1] <- NA
> > Nst <- array(NA, dim = dim(Rst))
> > tmp <- apply(data_matrix, 1, max, na.rm = TRUE)
> > tmp[tmp == '-Inf'] <- 2
> > Nst[,1] <- tmp
> >
> > # Initial values
> > inits <- function(){list(r = Rst, N = Nst+1, alpha.lam = rnorm(1, -1,1))}
> >
> > # Parameters monitored
> > params <-c("alpha.lam", "phi", "alpha.gamma", "beta.gamma", "sigma.gamma", "gamma0",
> > "alpha.p", "N", "K", "r")
> >
> > # MCMC settings
> > na <- 1000 ; ni <- 70000 ; nt <- 4 ; nb <- 10000 ; nc <- 4
> >
> > # try different seeds in hopes of getting one that runs
> > set.seed(299, kind = "Mersenne-Twister")
> >
> > out4 <- jags(bdata, inits, params, "gompertz_AHM2.jags", n.adapt = na, n.chains = nc,
> >              n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, parallel = TRUE)

messages.subject: what computer to buy ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

a colleague intending to attend a workshop just sent me this, as she said, "random question": "I am looking into buying a computer that would be suitable for running the IPM models and am trying to determine what specs would be best to include. Any information or suggestions you could provide would be greatly appreciated!". I thought this was quite a good question to ask in this forum, and therefore I copied this over.

My understanding is that if you want speed, then you want to have a lot of RAM (e.g., >=32 GB), quite a few cores (e.g., >= 8) and high CPU frequency. When I buy a new laptop I decide how much I can spend and then try to go as high as possible in these three things. Is this entirely naive ?

I think that one of those gamers' laptops may be quite good for running models; but their esthetics ..... ugh !

Thanks for comments.

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Re: what computer to buy ?
messages.body_plain:
Eh eh, no one takes serious when you arrive with a gaming laptop!

One problem with those machines is that they usually came with powerful sound and graphics cards. You don't need those to run HM's, so you end up buying something you don't need. Look for machines with the same processor a lower sound and graphics cards, they can be some hundreds of euros cheaper.

Cheers!
